title: Data Representation: Solubility and Temperature
text:
Solubility is the maximum mass of a solute that can dissolve in a given volume of solvent at a specified temperature. A solution that contains this maximum mass of dissolved solute is said to be saturated. If a saturated solution is cooled to a temperature at which the solubility is lower, the excess solute crystallizes out of the solution.

Students investigated how temperature affects the solubility in water of three ionic compounds: Salt A, Salt B, and Salt C. In each trial, a salt was added to 100 mL of distilled water held at a constant temperature in a water bath. The mixture was stirred until no additional solid would dissolve, and the mass of dissolved salt was determined. Each measurement was repeated three times, and the average values were recorded.

Table 1 shows the solubility of Salt A at six temperatures.

Table 1
Temperature (°C) | Solubility of Salt A (g/100 mL)
10 | 21
20 | 32
30 | 45
40 | 55
50 | 68
60 | 82

Table 2 shows the solubility of Salt B and Salt C at the same six temperatures.

Table 2
Temperature (°C) | Salt B (g/100 mL) | Salt C (g/100 mL)
10 | 35 | 60
20 | 36 | 54
30 | 37 | 49
40 | 38 | 43
50 | 39 | 38
60 | 40 | 33

The students noted that the solubility of Salt A increased rapidly with temperature, while the solubility of Salt B increased only slightly over the same range. In contrast, the solubility of Salt C decreased steadily as temperature increased, a behavior seen in some salts whose dissolving process releases heat. The students also observed that the water bath temperature had to be held within 0.5°C of the target value, because even small changes in temperature measurably changed the mass of Salt A that dissolved.

subject: science
title: Data Representation: Enzyme Activity, pH, and Temperature
text:
Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions in living cells. The activity of an enzyme (how quickly it converts reactant into product) is affected by the pH and the temperature of its surroundings. Each enzyme has an optimum pH and an optimum temperature at which its activity is greatest. Far from these optimum conditions, the enzyme's shape changes and its activity declines.

Biologists measured the activity of three digestive enzymes, Enzyme X, Enzyme Y, and Enzyme Z, in buffered solutions of different pH. All trials in this set were run at 30°C with equal enzyme and reactant concentrations. Activity was recorded as micromoles (µmol) of product formed per minute. The results are shown in Table 1.

Table 1
pH | Enzyme X (µmol/min) | Enzyme Y (µmol/min) | Enzyme Z (µmol/min)
2 | 45 | 2 | 0
4 | 30 | 10 | 5
6 | 8 | 42 | 18
8 | 1 | 25 | 40
10 | 0 | 6 | 22

Next, the biologists studied how temperature affects Enzyme Y. In these trials, the pH was held constant at 6 while the temperature was varied. All other conditions were the same as in the first set of trials. The results are shown in Table 2.

Table 2
Temperature (°C) | Enzyme Y activity (µmol/min)
10 | 12
20 | 25
30 | 42
40 | 48
50 | 15
60 | 2

The biologists noted that in the human body, different regions of the digestive tract maintain very different pH values. For example, the interior of the stomach is strongly acidic, with a pH near 2, while the small intestine is slightly basic, with a pH near 8. Enzymes secreted into each region are expected to work best at the pH of that region.

subject: science
title: Research Summaries: Period of a Simple Pendulum
text:
A simple pendulum consists of a small weight (a bob) hanging from a light string attached to a fixed support. The period of a pendulum is the time required for one complete back-and-forth swing. Students performed three experiments to determine which factors affect the period. In every trial, the students pulled the bob to the side, released it, timed 10 complete swings with a stopwatch, and divided the total time by 10 to find the period. Each trial was repeated three times and the results were averaged.

Experiment 1
The students attached a 50 g bob to strings of different lengths. In every trial, the bob was released from an angle of 10° from vertical. The results are shown in Table 1.

Table 1
String length (cm) | Period (s)
25 | 1.0
50 | 1.4
100 | 2.0
200 | 2.8

Experiment 2
The students used a string length of 100 cm and a release angle of 10°, but varied the mass of the bob. The results are shown in Table 2.

Table 2
Bob mass (g) | Period (s)
25 | 2.0
50 | 2.0
100 | 2.0
200 | 2.0

Experiment 3
The students used a string length of 100 cm and a 50 g bob, but varied the release angle. The results are shown in Table 3.

Table 3
Release angle (°) | Period (s)
5 | 2.0
10 | 2.0
20 | 2.0

The students noticed that in Experiment 1, each time the string length was doubled, the period increased by a factor of about 1.4. They concluded that, for the ranges tested, the period of a simple pendulum depends on the length of the string but not on the mass of the bob or the release angle. They designed the three experiments so that only one factor was changed at a time, allowing the effect of each factor to be evaluated separately.

subject: science
title: Data Representation: Stream Discharge and Sediment Transport
text:
Hydrologists monitored a stream at a gauging station for one year. Discharge is the volume of water flowing past a point per second, measured in cubic meters per second (m³/s). Suspended sediment concentration is the mass of fine particles carried in each liter of water, measured in milligrams per liter (mg/L). In this stream, the speed (velocity) of the flowing water increases as discharge increases. Table 1 shows the average discharge and suspended sediment concentration for six months of the year. Snowmelt in the surrounding mountains reaches its peak in late spring.

Table 1
Month | Discharge (m³/s) | Suspended sediment (mg/L)
January | 12 | 40
March | 45 | 180
May | 88 | 420
July | 30 | 120
September | 15 | 55
November | 20 | 75

The hydrologists also studied how water velocity determines the largest sediment particles a stream can move along its bed. Sediment particles are classified by size: silt particles are the smallest listed here, followed in increasing size by sand, gravel, and cobbles. Using a laboratory channel in which water velocity could be precisely controlled, the hydrologists determined the minimum velocity, in centimeters per second (cm/s), needed to transport each particle type. The results are shown in Table 2.

Table 2
Minimum water velocity (cm/s) | Largest particle type transported
10 | silt
30 | sand
75 | gravel
150 | cobbles

A velocity of at least 10 cm/s is required to move silt, and progressively higher velocities are required to move the larger particle types. At velocities between the listed values, the stream can transport all particle types whose minimum velocities have been reached, but none of the larger types. The hydrologists concluded that months with higher discharge are associated both with faster water and with higher suspended sediment concentrations, so the stream reshapes its bed most actively during high-discharge months.

subject: science
title: Research Summaries: Fertilizer and Tomato Seedling Growth
text:
Botanists studied how the nutrients nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) affect the growth of tomato seedlings. In each experiment, groups of 20 seedlings of the same variety were planted in identical pots containing the same base soil, given equal amounts of water, and kept under the same lighting and temperature conditions in a greenhouse. After 30 days, the height of each seedling was measured, and the mean (average) height for each group was calculated.

Experiment 1
The botanists mixed different amounts of nitrogen into the soil of each group. No phosphorus was added to any group in this experiment. The results are shown in Table 1.

Table 1
Nitrogen added (g/kg soil) | Mean height (cm)
0 | 12
1 | 18
2 | 24
4 | 29
8 | 22

The group receiving 8 g/kg of nitrogen showed yellowed leaf edges, a sign of nutrient stress caused by excess fertilizer.

Experiment 2
The botanists next studied phosphorus. Every group in this experiment received 2 g/kg of nitrogen, and different amounts of phosphorus were mixed into the soil of each group. All other conditions were the same as in Experiment 1. The results are shown in Table 2.

Table 2
Phosphorus added (g/kg soil) | Mean height (cm)
0 | 24
1 | 28
2 | 31
4 | 32

The botanists noted that the group in Experiment 2 that received no phosphorus grew to the same mean height (24 cm) as the Experiment 1 group that received 2 g/kg of nitrogen alone, as expected, since the two groups were treated identically. They concluded that moderate nitrogen additions increased seedling height, that nitrogen additions beyond 4 g/kg reduced growth, and that phosphorus additions further increased height, although the benefit of phosphorus leveled off at the higher amounts tested. The botanists planned a future experiment to test the effect of potassium on seedling growth.

subject: science
title: Conflicting Viewpoints: The End-Cretaceous Extinction
text:
About 66 million years ago, at the end of the Cretaceous Period, roughly three-quarters of Earth's plant and animal species, including all dinosaurs except birds, became extinct. A thin layer of clay found worldwide at rock layers of this age is unusually rich in iridium, an element that is rare in Earth's crust. Two scientists discuss the cause of the extinction.

Scientist 1
The extinction was caused by the impact of an asteroid roughly 10 km in diameter. The impact blasted enormous quantities of vaporized rock, dust, and sulfur droplets into the atmosphere, blocking sunlight worldwide for months. Photosynthesis nearly stopped, food webs collapsed, and species died out abruptly. Asteroids are rich in iridium, so the worldwide iridium layer represents fallout from the impact. The same clay layer contains shocked quartz grains and tiny glass spherules, which form only under the sudden, extreme pressures and temperatures of an impact; ordinary volcanic eruptions cannot produce shocked quartz. A buried impact crater about 180 km wide exists on the Yucatán Peninsula, and its age matches the age of the boundary layer. The abruptness of the extinction, with many species disappearing at exactly the level of the iridium layer, is exactly what an impact predicts.

Scientist 2
The extinction was caused primarily by enormous volcanic eruptions in the region that is now India, which began about 400,000 years before the boundary layer was deposited and continued afterward. These eruptions released vast amounts of carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide. The carbon dioxide caused episodes of climate warming, while sulfur droplets periodically blocked sunlight, cooled the surface, and produced acid rain that stressed ocean ecosystems. Because these stresses accumulated over hundreds of thousands of years, species declined gradually, and the fossil record shows that many groups were already dwindling well before the boundary. Iridium is also delivered to the surface by plumes of material rising from Earth's deep mantle, so gases and particles from these mantle-fed eruptions could have deposited the iridium layer over many millennia. An impact may have occurred, but it merely finished off ecosystems that volcanism had already pushed to the edge of collapse.

subject: science
title: Data Representation: Properties of Stars
text:
Astronomers compiled data on four stars, labeled Star A through Star D. Each star's surface temperature was determined from its spectrum, and its color was recorded. Luminosity is the total amount of energy a star emits per second, expressed here relative to the Sun (Sun = 1). A star's luminosity depends on both its surface temperature and its surface area: hotter stars emit more energy per unit of area, and larger stars have more emitting area. The four stars in Table 1 are all main-sequence stars, a class of stars in which luminosity consistently increases with surface temperature.

Table 1
Star | Surface temperature (K) | Color | Luminosity (Sun = 1)
Star A | 3,200 | red | 0.04
Star B | 5,800 | yellow | 1.0
Star C | 9,900 | white | 25
Star D | 25,000 | blue | 8,000

Apparent brightness is how bright a star looks from Earth. It depends on the star's luminosity and on its distance: light spreads out as it travels, so a star looks dimmer the farther away it is. To isolate the effect of distance, astronomers calculated the apparent brightness of identical stars, each with the same luminosity as Star B, placed at different distances from Earth. Apparent brightness is given in relative units, with the value at 10 light-years defined as 100. The results are shown in Table 2.

Table 2
Distance (light-years) | Apparent brightness (relative units)
10 | 100
20 | 25
40 | 6.3
80 | 1.6

The data in Table 2 show that each time the distance to a star is doubled, its apparent brightness decreases by a factor of 4. Because of this rapid decrease, a highly luminous star that is very distant can appear dimmer from Earth than a much less luminous star that is nearby. Astronomers must therefore know a star's distance before they can use its apparent brightness to determine its luminosity.

subject: science
title: Research Summaries: Rates of a Chemical Reaction
text:
When marble chips (calcium carbonate) are placed in hydrochloric acid (HCl), the mixture fizzes as carbon dioxide gas (CO2) is produced. Students measured the rate of this reaction by timing how long it took to collect 50 mL of CO2 in a gas syringe. A shorter collection time indicates a faster reaction. In every trial, 5.0 g of marble chips were added to 50 mL of acid, and the same apparatus was used.

Experiment 1
The students varied the concentration of the HCl. All trials were run at 20°C using medium-sized marble chips. The results are shown in Table 1.

Table 1
HCl concentration (M) | Time to collect 50 mL of CO2 (s)
0.5 | 240
1.0 | 118
1.5 | 80
2.0 | 61

Experiment 2
The students varied the temperature of the acid. All trials used 1.0 M HCl and medium-sized marble chips. The results are shown in Table 2.

Table 2
Temperature (°C) | Time to collect 50 mL of CO2 (s)
10 | 236
20 | 118
30 | 60
40 | 31

Experiment 3
The students varied the size of the marble chips, keeping the total mass at 5.0 g. All trials used 1.0 M HCl at 20°C. Smaller pieces of a solid expose more total surface area to the acid. The results are shown in Table 3.

Table 3
Marble chip size | Time to collect 50 mL of CO2 (s)
large chips | 190
medium chips | 118
powder | 22

The students concluded that the reaction proceeded faster when the acid was more concentrated, when the temperature was higher, and when the marble was more finely divided. They explained these results using collision theory: reactions occur when reactant particles collide, so conditions that produce more frequent or more energetic collisions between acid particles and the marble surface increase the reaction rate.

subject: science
title: Data Representation: Pressure, Volume, and Temperature of a Gas
text:
Students studied the behavior of a fixed sample of air (0.010 mol) sealed in a cylinder fitted with a movable piston. The volume of the gas could be read from a scale on the cylinder, the pressure could be adjusted by adding weights to the piston, and the temperature could be controlled by placing the cylinder in a water bath. Temperature was recorded in kelvins (K); a temperature of 0 K, called absolute zero, is the lowest temperature possible.

Study 1
The students held the temperature of the gas constant at 293 K and measured the volume of the gas at four different pressures, in kilopascals (kPa). The results are shown in Table 1.

Table 1
Pressure (kPa) | Volume (mL)
50 | 480
100 | 240
150 | 160
200 | 120

The students noticed that for every row of Table 1, the product of pressure and volume was the same: 24,000 kPa·mL. Whenever the pressure was doubled, the volume was halved.

Study 2
The students held the pressure of the gas constant at 100 kPa and measured the volume of the gas at four different temperatures. The results are shown in Table 2.

Table 2
Temperature (K) | Volume (mL)
200 | 164
250 | 205
300 | 246
350 | 287

In Study 2, the volume increased by the same amount, 41 mL, for every 50 K increase in temperature. When the students plotted volume versus temperature, the data points fell on a straight line. Extending this line backward toward lower and lower temperatures, the students observed that the line pointed toward a volume of 0 mL at a temperature of 0 K. Real gases condense into liquids before reaching such low temperatures, so the line cannot be followed all the way to 0 K in practice. The students noted that their two studies examined the two pressure-volume-temperature relationships separately: Study 1 examined pressure and volume at constant temperature, while Study 2 examined temperature and volume at constant pressure.

subject: science
title: Research Summaries: Antibiotic Effectiveness
text:
Microbiologists tested antibiotics using the disk diffusion method. A petri dish containing a nutrient gel is evenly coated with bacteria. Small paper disks, each soaked with a known amount of an antibiotic, are placed on the gel, and the dish is kept at 37°C for 24 hours. Bacteria grow to cover the gel except in a clear circular region, called the zone of inhibition, around any disk whose antibiotic stops bacterial growth. A larger zone diameter indicates a more effective antibiotic; a zone diameter of 0 mm means bacteria grew right up to the edge of the disk.

Experiment 1
Disks containing 20 µg of Antibiotic A, B, C, or D were tested against the bacterium E. coli. The results are shown in Table 1.

Table 1
Antibiotic (20 µg) | Zone diameter (mm)
A | 22
B | 8
C | 15
D | 0

Experiment 2
Disks containing different amounts of Antibiotic A were tested against E. coli. All other procedures were identical to those of Experiment 1. The results are shown in Table 2.

Table 2
Amount of Antibiotic A (µg/disk) | Zone diameter (mm)
5 | 10
10 | 15
20 | 22
40 | 28

Experiment 3
Disks containing 20 µg of Antibiotic A were tested against four different species of bacteria. All other procedures were identical to those of Experiment 1. The results are shown in Table 3.

Table 3
Bacterial species | Zone diameter (mm)
E. coli | 22
S. aureus | 25
P. aeruginosa | 6
B. subtilis | 24

In every experiment, one additional disk soaked only in sterile water was placed on each dish. The microbiologists concluded that the four antibiotics differed greatly in effectiveness against E. coli, that larger amounts of Antibiotic A produced larger zones of inhibition, and that the effectiveness of Antibiotic A varied considerably among bacterial species.

subject: science
title: Conflicting Viewpoints: The Origin of the Moon
text:
The Moon has several properties that any explanation of its origin must account for. The Moon's overall density is much lower than Earth's, and its iron core is unusually small for a body of its size. Oxygen atoms in Moon rocks occur in nearly identical isotope ratios to those in Earth rocks, whereas rocks from Mars and from most asteroids have distinctly different ratios. Finally, the Moon's ancient crust is made of a rock type that forms when minerals float to the top of a deep, planet-wide ocean of molten rock, so the young Moon must once have been almost entirely molten. Two scientists present hypotheses for the Moon's origin.

Scientist 1
About 4.5 billion years ago, a planet-sized body roughly the size of Mars collided with the young Earth. The colliding body's iron core sank and merged with Earth's core, while rocky material from the outer layers of both bodies was blasted into orbit. This orbiting debris quickly gathered together to form the Moon. Because the debris came mostly from the iron-poor outer rocky layers, the Moon ended up with only a small iron core. Because material from Earth and the impactor was vaporized and thoroughly mixed, Moon rocks and Earth rocks have nearly identical oxygen isotope ratios. The enormous energy of the collision melted the newly formed Moon, producing the molten state recorded by its ancient crust.

Scientist 2
The Moon formed as a separate, independent body from iron-poor material orbiting in the same region of the early solar system as Earth. Because it formed from the same local material as Earth, its rocks naturally have oxygen isotope ratios similar to Earth's. The Moon later passed close to Earth and was captured into orbit. Capture is difficult because an approaching body normally passes by or collides; the Moon was slowed just enough by friction with the thick, extended atmosphere that surrounded the young Earth. The heat generated during capture, together with heat from later impacts, melted the young Moon, producing its ancient molten state. A giant collision is not required to explain any of the Moon's properties.

subject: science
title: Research Summaries: Friction on an Inclined Plane
text:
When a block rests on a ramp, friction between the block and the ramp surface keeps the block from sliding. If one end of the ramp is slowly raised, the block eventually begins to slide. The angle of the ramp at the moment sliding begins is a measure of the friction between the two surfaces: the greater the friction, the larger the angle that can be reached before sliding starts. Students investigated friction using a wooden ramp hinged at one end. In each trial, a block was placed on the ramp, the free end of the ramp was raised slowly, and the angle at which the block began to slide was recorded. Each trial was repeated three times and the results were averaged.

Experiment 1
Four blocks, each with a mass of 200 g, were tested. The blocks were identical except for the material covering their bottom surfaces. The results are shown in Table 1.

Table 1
Bottom surface of block | Angle at which sliding began (°)
rubber | 42
wood | 27
metal | 22
Teflon | 8

Experiment 2
A wood-bottomed block was tested with different masses stacked on top of it. The total mass for each trial is listed in Table 2.

Table 2
Total mass (g) | Angle at which sliding began (°)
100 | 27
200 | 27
400 | 28
800 | 27

Experiment 3
A rectangular wood-bottomed block of mass 200 g was rested on each of its three different faces, so that the area of contact with the ramp differed among trials. The results are shown in Table 3.

Table 3
Face in contact | Contact area (cm²) | Angle at which sliding began (°)
small | 24 | 27
medium | 48 | 27
large | 96 | 27

The students concluded that the sliding angle depended strongly on the materials in contact but was essentially unaffected, within the precision of their measurements, by the mass of the block or by the area of contact between the block and the ramp.

subject: science
title: Data Representation: Ocean Depth Profiles
text:
Oceanographers lowered an instrument package from a research ship at a single station in the tropical Atlantic Ocean. The instruments recorded water temperature, salinity (the mass of dissolved salt per 1,000 g of seawater, in parts per thousand, ppt), and density at various depths. The results are shown in Table 1.

Table 1
Depth (m) | Temperature (°C) | Salinity (ppt) | Density (g/cm³)
0 | 24 | 35.0 | 1.0235
200 | 18 | 35.5 | 1.0258
600 | 8 | 34.8 | 1.0271
1,000 | 5 | 34.7 | 1.0278
2,000 | 3 | 34.7 | 1.0282

The density of seawater increases when its temperature decreases and also increases when its salinity increases. At this station, density increased continuously with depth even across depth ranges in which salinity decreased slightly, because the effect of the falling temperature outweighed the effect of the small salinity changes. The zone of rapid temperature decrease that separates warm surface water from cold deep water is called the thermocline.

The oceanographers also measured how much sunlight penetrates the water column. Light intensity at each depth is expressed as a percentage of the intensity at the surface. The results are shown in Table 2.

Table 2
Depth (m) | Light intensity (% of surface)
0 | 100
50 | 25
100 | 3
200 | 0.1

Photosynthetic organisms, such as the microscopic algae that form the base of the ocean food web, generally require a light intensity of at least 1% of the surface value to grow. The layer of the ocean in which light is sufficient for photosynthesis is called the photic zone. Below the photic zone, organisms must rely on food that sinks from above or on other energy sources. The oceanographers noted that both the temperature structure and the light structure of the water column help determine where marine organisms can live.

subject: science
title: Research Summaries: Water Retention in Soils
text:
Soils are composed of mineral particles of different sizes. Of the particle types studied here, sand grains are the largest, silt particles are intermediate, and clay particles are the smallest. Loam is a natural soil containing a mixture of sand, silt, and clay. Students investigated how soil composition affects the movement and storage of water.

Experiment 1
A funnel lined with fine mesh was filled with 200 g of a dry soil and placed over a graduated cylinder. Then 100 mL of water was poured evenly over the soil. After water stopped dripping from the funnel, the volume of drained water in the cylinder was recorded. The volume of water retained by the soil was calculated by subtracting the drained volume from 100 mL. The procedure was repeated for each soil. The results are shown in Table 1.

Table 1
Soil | Water drained (mL) | Water retained (mL)
sand | 82 | 18
silt | 55 | 45
clay | 30 | 70
loam | 48 | 52

Experiment 2
The procedure of Experiment 1 was repeated, and for each soil the students also measured the time from the start of pouring until dripping stopped. The results are shown in Table 2.

Table 2
Soil | Time until dripping stopped (s)
sand | 35
silt | 190
clay | 940
loam | 210

Experiment 3
The students prepared 200 g mixtures of sand and clay in different proportions and measured water retention using the procedure of Experiment 1. The results are shown in Table 3.

Table 3
Clay in mixture (% by mass) | Water retained (mL)
0 | 18
25 | 33
50 | 46
75 | 58
100 | 70

The students concluded that soils made of smaller particles retained more water and drained more slowly than soils made of larger particles, and that adding clay to sand steadily increased the amount of water the mixture retained. They noted that plants generally grow best in soils that hold enough water for roots to absorb but that also drain quickly enough to let air reach the roots.

subject: science
title: Conflicting Viewpoints: How Migrating Birds Navigate
text:
Many bird species migrate thousands of kilometers each year, often returning to the same breeding and wintering sites. How birds find their way remains an active area of research. Three students each propose a primary mechanism of bird navigation.

Student 1
Birds navigate primarily by sensing Earth's magnetic field. Tiny crystals of magnetite, a magnetic mineral, occur in the beaks of many birds, and specialized molecules in birds' eyes respond to magnetic fields. The strength and tilt of the magnetic field vary predictably with latitude, so the field provides both a compass and information about position. A magnetic sense works during the day or night and in any weather, which explains why caged migratory birds still orient in the correct migratory direction on completely overcast nights, when no sun or stars are visible. When researchers surround caged birds with electric coils that shift the direction of the local magnetic field, the birds shift their orientation by the same amount.

Student 2
Birds navigate primarily by celestial cues. During the day, birds use the position of the sun, adjusting for the time of day with their internal biological clock. At night, birds use the star patterns that rotate around a fixed point in the sky, which marks a constant direction. When caged birds are placed in a planetarium and the projected star pattern is rotated to a new orientation, the birds change their migratory orientation to match the projected sky rather than the true sky. Celestial cues are unavailable under heavy cloud cover, but birds can simply pause migration until the sky clears.

Student 3
Birds navigate primarily by using learned information about the landscape. Birds memorize the positions of rivers, coastlines, mountain ridges, and other landmarks, and some birds also learn the characteristic odors carried on winds from different regions. Young birds learn migration routes by traveling with experienced members of their flock. This explains why, in some species, young birds migrating alone for the first time are far more likely to wander off course than adults, and why birds often follow coastlines and river valleys rather than flying in straight lines toward their destinations.
